issuing_body: Legal Subcommittee of the Copyright Subdivision, Council for Cultural Affairs (Agency for Cultural Affairs, Japan) / 文化審議会著作権分科会法制度小委員会
covered_actors: AI service providers (AIサービス提供事業者)
AI users, including businesses and individuals (AI利用者)
Copyright holders, creators, and performers (クリエイターや実演家等の権利者)
Content posting platform operators (コンテンツ投稿プラットフォーム事業者)
penalties_summary: When AI training, generation, or utilization constitutes copyright infringement outside statutory exceptions, existing legal remedies under Japan's Copyright Act and Civil Code apply: civil damages (Civil Code Art. 709, requiring intent or negligence), injunctions including cessation/prevention, removal of works from future training datasets, technical preventive measures, or disposal of infringing outputs and—in limited cases—trained models (Copyright Act Art. 112(1)–(2)), criminal penalties for intentional infringement (Copyright Act Art. 119), and unjust enrichment restitution even absent intent or negligence. Falsely licensing non-copyrightable AI outputs as copyrighted works may also incur contractual, civil tort, or criminal fraud liability.
implementation_notes: The document explicitly states that it has no legal binding force and does not make definitive legal determinations on specific generative AI systems; copyright law is private law interpreted case-by-case by courts. It provides interpretive guidance on Japan's Copyright Act (notably Arts. 30-4 and 47-5) across the development/training stage (coexisting enjoyment purpose such as intentional overfitting or certain RAG uses, and the proviso against unreasonably prejudicing copyright owners' interests, including paid info-analysis databases, technical access restrictions like robots.txt, and pirate sites), the generation/utilization stage (similarity, reliance, and normative liability of developers/providers), and copyrightability of AI-generated outputs. The Subcommittee and Agency for Cultural Affairs plan ongoing case collection, public outreach, and future updates as jurisprudence and technology evolve.
